title: Paris Sets Curfews After Weekend of Protests and Rioting
summary:
Police in Paris, France, set an overnight curfew on Monday in two parts of the city. The goal was to prevent more violence after a weekend of rioting that the report called France's worst in years.

The trouble began during nationwide protests on Saturday. People were protesting against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. Mass protests in France are often peaceful, but violence on the edges of some marches led to clashes with police. Rioters targeted city halls, other public buildings and thousands of businesses. Authorities estimated that at least 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted, and at least 2,400 people were arrested across the country.

The Paris curfew covered the Place de la République, a large public square, and Les Halles, a shopping area. It lasted from 11 p.m. Monday until 6 a.m. Tuesday. Gatherings and demonstrations were also banned from 8 p.m.

Some cities made special rules for young people. In northern France, several cities, including Lille, set a curfew for children and teenagers under 18 from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. for a few days. Nice, on the French Riviera, also set an overnight curfew for minors.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had called for "very limited" and "localized" curfews. He defended how police handled the unrest and said no one was killed.

France's interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, offered to resign on Sunday, but President Emmanuel Macron refused. Macron asked him to be fully open about "failures in planning and intelligence-gathering" that led to the violence. Macron also asked for new policing methods to end the unrest as quickly as possible.

Lecornu said details of the curfews would be shared after talks with city mayors.
why_it_matters: The protests show how worries about prices and schools can lead to large public anger, and how governments try to restore safety while still allowing people to speak out.

background_read: In France, the president is the head of state, while the prime minister leads the government and the interior minister is in charge of police and public safety.
Large street protests are a common way for people in France to show anger about government decisions, prices or public services such as schools.
Most protest marches are peaceful, but when small groups turn violent, officials sometimes use curfews to keep people off the streets at night.
A curfew is meant to be temporary, giving police time to restore calm while leaders look into what went wrong.
